episode.title: Cariboo Signals - Indigenous Lands & Innovation
episode.description:
Riley and Casey explore technology and society in rural communities. Today's focus: Indigenous Lands & Innovation.

THIS WEEK WE'RE ASKING: Is staying put a virtue or a failure of nerve?

NEWS ROUNDUP: We break down Doerkson orders B.C. public service to implement return -to-office plan and Public service union calls on Liberals to criminalize residential school denialism, plus 10 more stories, and explore what these developments mean for communities like ours.

RURAL CONNECTIONS: Deep dive on Indigenous Lands & Innovation Topics include: AI, funding.

Hosts: Riley (Tech optimist with an engineering background) and Casey (Community-first skeptic of tech promises).

COMMUNITY SPOTLIGHT: Denisiqi Services Society

research.block:
PRE-RESEARCHED INSIGHTS FOR THE DEEP DIVE

RESEARCH QUESTION: What is the state of opposition to Bill C-39 (the Building Canada Strong Act), and what does the bill actually change?

Findings: Opposition is broad and organized, not limited to the Attawapiskat youth. The Chiefs of Ontario, AFN Quebec-Labrador, BC Assembly of First Nations and Nishnawbe Aski Nation issued a joint rejection on October 8, 2026, titled "Rights Cannot Be Fast-Tracked." The AFN has called the bill "fundamentally flawed" and wants several sections withdrawn entirely, with no room for amendments. The UBCIC warned in a submission that the emphasis on accelerated reviews and a one-year timeline for project decisions risks leaving the Crown unable to meet its constitutional duties to consult. Matawa First Nations told a House of Commons committee the bill is "legislative coercion." The Narwhal reports senators questioning its impact on First Nations. The bill is an omnibus measure that reshapes Indigenous consultation for mining, oil and gas and infrastructure, and shortens environmental review. Several First Nations assemblies have also passed their own rejections.
Suggested angle: Riley can argue that a one-year decision clock and a single coordinated review are the kind of permitting reform Canada needs, and that Indigenous communities could be given a seat in faster processes. Casey can respond that the complaint is about process and rights, not speed alone. The UBCIC's point that a compressed timeline may make the Crown unable to satisfy its own constitutional duty turns "efficiency" into a legal liability. Use the joint chiefs' statement and the AFN's call for withdrawal as evidence that the opposition is institutional, which makes the December 8 protest a bargaining signal, not a fringe action.

RESEARCH QUESTION: Does the KSM ruling show that court-ordered consultation can stall a major mine, and what exactly was decided?

Findings: On November 18, 2026, B.C. Supreme Court Justice Emily Burke clarified a June ruling. The province must "engage in deep consultation" with the Tsetsaut Skii km Lax Ha Nation before reconsidering whether Seabridge Gold's KSM project had "substantially started" construction in 2024. The court quashed the 2024 designation. Coverage from Mining.com and The Northern Miner says the environmental assessment approval itself is unaffected, according to Seabridge's own statement. Seabridge says it will check with the Environmental Assessment Office on whether the ruling affects timing. Seabridge's stock fell on the news.
Suggested angle: This is a strong test case for the bill debate. Riley can point out that the mine already has an environmental approval and that the setback is about a procedural designation, so the system is working and the dispute is narrow. Casey can counter that the ruling shows a small nation's consultation rights carry real legal weight, and that a bill compressing those steps could produce more cases like this, not fewer. Note that the court left the EA approval intact, so both sides can claim the outcome supports their view. Be careful to describe this as a reconsideration order, not a cancellation of the project.

RESEARCH QUESTION: Are Indigenous-led resource partnerships, such as the BHP Foundation deal, a path to Indigenous equity or a way to smooth approvals for industry?

Findings: The First Nations Major Projects Coalition has signed a C$5.6 million (about US$3.9 million) multi-year partnership with the BHP Foundation, running through March 2031. The stated purpose is to strengthen First Nations' negotiating capacity and help them structure their involvement in major projects. The Logic describes the aim as helping First Nations negotiate equity stakes in resource projects. Coverage frames the deal as support for First Nations "shaping major projects on their own terms."
Suggested angle: This is the most interesting tension in the episode. Riley can argue that Indigenous equity ownership and negotiating capacity are the real innovation, and that funding from a mining company is a practical route to economic self-determination. Casey can ask who sets the terms: a mining company funding the advisers who negotiate with that same industry raises questions of independence. The useful question for the deep dive is whether the coalition's funding is for capacity or for deal-making, and who ultimately decides. Note that the coalition is a partner of the federal push for faster approvals, so the same organization may be both a beneficiary and a critic of Bill C-39's timelines.

RESEARCH QUESTION: How are tribes in the United States using legal sovereignty claims against prediction markets, and does the Canadian pattern apply?

Findings: The NYT reports that eight tribes have sued Kalshi over the past 18 months to bar it from their lands, arguing that tribal sovereignty lets them decide what gaming is allowed. On November 4, 2026, U.S. District Judge Jacqueline Scott Corley granted a preliminary injunction to Blue Lake Rancheria and Chicken Ranch Rancheria of Me-Wuk Indians, blocking Kalshi's sports event contracts on those tribal lands. The injunction followed a September 2026 Ninth Circuit ruling that the tribes were likely to succeed on claims under the Indian Gaming Regulatory Act. The injunction covers tribal land, not the state as a whole. A Ninth Circuit ruling also rejected a Lanham Act claim on the contracts' legality.
Suggested angle: This is a comparable case for a segment about Indigenous sovereignty as a tool for controlling new technology. Riley can present the tribes as proof that sovereignty law can govern digital markets, with an injunction in hand. Casey can point out that the wins are narrow, limited to tribal land and specific contracts, and that the tribes depend on a single federal statute. Use it to show that Indigenous rights frameworks can be a brake on fast-moving tech, the same way Bill C-39 critics argue for consultation as a brake on fast-moving approvals. The contrast is that here the tribes are the ones seeking to slow an innovation, and the question is whether they get to set the terms.

roundup.opening_frame: A news day where a new B.C. government is moving fast on public service, schools and Indigenous rights, while Indigenous nations from Alberta to Greenland to Brazil press on who gets to decide.

stories.point: Premier Lorne Doerkson has ordered the B.C. public service head, Kim Henderson, to begin a phased return-to-office plan, with public servants who can work from the office back five days a week.
stories.bridge_to_next: Same new Doerkson government, same week of orders: from the office to the classroom.

stories.point: Doerkson is directing the Education Ministry to remove all SOGI 123 material from government websites and to work with districts to remove it from classrooms, and the B.C. Teachers' Federation says it is disappointed.
Quesnel's City Furniture, run by the Wander family since 1992, is marking 34 years under Jack and Rami and the franchise's 50th anniversary.
The Public Service Alliance of Canada is echoing Indigenous leaders and the Assembly of First Nations in calling on Ottawa to criminalize residential school denialism.
stories.bridge_to_next: Moving from the residential school record to the question of who decides: First Nations jurisdiction, which Alberta's separatism referendum put to the test.

stories.point: A Yellowhead Institute brief says First Nations challenged Alberta separatism through litigation and public mobilization, arguing Alberta's future cannot be decided without Indigenous jurisdiction and treaty relationships.
stories.bridge_to_next: Provincial politics and Indigenous rights: back to B.C., where the new government's promise to repeal DRIPA is the next flashpoint.

stories.point: First Nations Summit's Robert Phillips says repealing DRIPA could have dire consequences in courts and possibly direct action, though he is open to talks with Doerkson; the Globe's summary adds that Doerkson's mandate letters direct cabinet to reverse Indigenous rights, climate and drug policies.
stories.bridge_to_next: From provincial law to a federal one: the clean water bill and who is recognized as holding rights.

stories.point: The AFN's national chief says the federal First Nations Clean Water Act, Bill C-37, falls short because it does not recognize a human right to water, unlike the earlier Bill C-61.
stories.bridge_to_next: Federal programs for Indigenous communities: from a bill the AFN says is too weak to an Inuit-led program that Inuit organizations will design themselves.

stories.point: The Pirutsiagutiit framework will replace the interim Inuit Child First Initiative on April 1, 2027, with $575 million proposed over five years, and four Inuit treaty organizations will co-develop regional approaches.
stories.bridge_to_next: Indigenous peoples defending their own territories: from Inuit-led programs to the Asháninka in Peru.

stories.point: The Asháninka, armed decades ago to fight Shining Path rebels, are still defending their Amazon rainforest, now against cocaine traffickers, without outside help.
stories.bridge_to_next: Another Amazon-region Indigenous people under pressure on their land: the isolated Awá in Brazil.

stories.point: About 20 isolated Awá approached the Guajajara village of Tawari in Brazil's Arariboia territory, and the government activated emergency coordination while stating its policy is to protect the Awá's right to remain isolated.
stories.bridge_to_next: Indigenous self-determination in a security setting: Greenland and the U.S. military pact.

stories.point: Denmark's parliament ratified the security agreement with Greenland and the U.S., which reaffirms Greenlanders' right to self-determination and stays in force if Greenland becomes independent; this is a U.S. policy matter, not ours to vote on, but worth watching for precedent.
stories.bridge_to_next: Coastal danger: from a pact on the Arctic to storm tides hitting the Pacific coast.

stories.point: Squamish declared a local state of emergency and communities across B.C., including the Tla-o-qui-aht First Nation, issued evacuation alerts as king tides, storm surge and heavy rain threatened the coast.
stories.bridge_to_next: Same tides, farther south: California's record high tides.

stories.point: Record high tides hit San Diego, Santa Barbara and Monterey on Wednesday, forcing some residents to flee and collapsing part of a pier.
The International Court of Justice has begun three weeks of argument in the first case of its kind on whether Myanmar committed genocide against the Rohingya.
A WIRED and Proof News investigation found gig nurses from apps like ShiftKey often get little or no onboarding in nursing homes, which can lead to dangerous mistakes.
Denmark's Supreme Court is set to rule on whether families can be forced from their homes under a law that divides residents into 'Western' and 'non-Western'.
Twenty-five years after Eritrea's 'Black Tuesday' arrests, families of the 'Eritrea 16' journalists do not know whether they are alive, and colleagues in Nairobi paid tribute to them.

roundup.handoff: Who holds the pen when Nations, provinces and Ottawa disagree, and what happens when a Nation sets its own terms on projects and revenue.

deep_dive.central_question: When First Nations in Canada and the U.S. try to set the terms of major projects and revenue themselves, does a funded seat at the table amount to real decision-making power, or does the power stay with whoever writes the rules, approves the projects and funds the capacity? And for the young people who come home to hold that work, is it a duty to the Nation or a burden the Nation should not have to carry?
deep_dive.riley_holds: Riley holds that Nations setting the terms of partnerships and revenue, with capacity built through coalitions and wins in court, is the practical route to real sovereignty, and that young people who return to staff that work are exercising a genuine claim, not a sacrifice.
deep_dive.casey_holds: Casey holds that a seat at the table is not authority, that funded capacity and consultation hubs can leave the final say with Ottawa or the province, and that asking returning youth to carry this work for their Nations treats a structural gap as a personal duty.

beats.claim: Sovereignty over revenue is being tested in court, and Nations that build legal capacity can win: tribes treat their gambling revenue as the base of their self-government and are fighting Kalshi's prediction markets over it.
beats.evidence: NYT Business: many U.S. tribes have relied on casinos and gambling revenue for survival; the tribal association of 62 tribes heard legal updates described as 'mostly favorable'; Blue Lake Rancheria recently won an injunction against Kalshi; tribes argue prediction markets threaten their sovereignty.
beats.pushback: Casey: a win in one court is a defence of existing revenue, not a model for new revenue terms; the same piece shows tribes had to organize as an association and litigate just to hold what they had, which takes lawyers and people who stay to run the case.
beats.leads_to_next: If revenue terms are defended case by case, the question becomes whether Canadian Nations can set terms before a project is approved rather than after, which is where the major-projects coalition comes in.

beats.claim: Canadian Nations are building shared negotiating capacity so they set the terms of major projects instead of reacting to them.
beats.evidence: Mining.com: the First Nations Major Projects Coalition has a multi-year partnership with the BHP Foundation worth $5.6 million (US$3.9 million) to strengthen negotiations and structure First Nations involvement in major projects.
beats.pushback: Casey: the money for the negotiating capacity comes from a mining company's foundation, so the Nations are building their bargaining strength with funding from a party they may sit across the table from; the article describes structure and involvement, not who holds a veto.
beats.leads_to_next: Funded capacity only matters if the law lets a Nation say no or insist on its terms, so the next beat looks at what the federal projects bill does to that power.

beats.claim: Whether a Nation can say no depends on law, and Bill C-39 shortens federal reviews while leaving consent language weak, which is why youth are mobilizing against it.
beats.evidence: Winnipeg Free Press: Attawapiskat youth plan a Dec. 8 day of action in Ottawa against Bill C-39; Liberal MPs rejected most NDP proposals to strengthen references to Indigenous rights and consent; the Liberals point to a proposed Crown Consultation Hub and say the duty to consult is preserved; officials told the committee they did not expect the bill to rush consultation. Idle No More and Onion Lake First Nation back the day of action.
beats.pushback: Riley: the government's stated design is for work with affected communities to begin well before a project reaches the regulator, and a hub could give Nations a front-loaded role; the test is whether Nations can hold that process to its word, not whether faster review is bad in itself.
beats.leads_to_next: If young people are the ones pressing on the law, the question is what they are being asked to carry, which the KSM mine ruling shows in a small Nation's fight over consultation.

beats.claim: A small Nation's insistence on deep consultation changed a provincial decision, showing that the power to say 'not yet' is real but has to be exercised by someone with the time and expertise to do it.
beats.evidence: Vancouver Sun: B.C. must 'engage in deep consultation' with a small northwest First Nation before reconsidering a 2024 decision that Seabridge Gold had 'substantially started' construction on its KSM project near Stewart.
beats.pushback: Riley: this is the kind of outcome Nations can win when they have counsel and the courts behind them, and it argues for investing in people who stay to do the work.
beats.leads_to_next: A win like this rests on a small Nation having people able to keep a file alive for years, which brings up the young people who return to do it and whether the arrangement should depend on them.

beats.claim: The youth organizing against C-39 are a sign that returning and staying to do governance work is both a claim on the future and a load placed on young people.
beats.evidence: Winnipeg Free Press: youth leader Jeronimo Kataquapit said 'We have to draw a line in the sand and say, No more'; organizer Ramon Kataquapit (APTN) said they planned to keep a presence on Parliament Hill.
beats.pushback: Casey: these youth are doing unpaid political work because the consultation process did not protect their Nations' interests, so framing it as duty lets the Crown off the hook; a system that needed this much mobilization has already failed.
beats.leads_to_next: If the burden is structural, the last beat asks what a Cariboo Nation's own terms look like and who staffs them.

beats.claim: The Cariboo answer is that holding a place together and setting the terms of its development are the same job, and the Nation should decide who does it and how it is paid for.
beats.evidence: Common public knowledge: Tŝilhqot'in Nation holds Aboriginal title after the 2014 Supreme Court of Canada ruling, and Williams Lake First Nation (Secwépemc) has been part of a regional mining and education agreement discussion; no new facts beyond today's articles.
beats.leads_to_next: Both hosts agree the Nation sets the terms, which leaves the structural question of who carries the staffing load and who holds the final word as the landing.

set_aside: Kalshi dispute as a separate gambling story, beyond its use as a revenue-sovereignty example
deep_dive.cariboo_beat: The last beat brings it home to the Tŝilhqot'in Nation, which holds Aboriginal title after the 2014 Supreme Court of Canada ruling, and to Secwépemc communities such as Williams Lake First Nation, asking who staffs governance and negotiation work in a Nation that sets its own terms, and whether returning youth are answering a duty or filling a gap that structure should fill.
deep_dive.landing: Held open: if a Nation holds title and sets the terms of partnerships, should its governance work rest on returning young people's choice to stay, or on institutions built so that no one has to sacrifice to keep the final say?
